_meta.description: Stage LR data path (a): genuine second candidates generated by the live reformulate() pipeline (top choice excluded, real gate stack re-run, not hand-picked), judged A-vs-B for the specific profile each was generated against.
_meta.method: stage_lr/generate_pairs.py — see LEARNED_REFORMULATION_RESEARCH.md's LR.1 data-path-(a) section for the full method, integrity fixes, and honest counts.

batch_2_r10.source: eval/r10_raw_results.json (Phase 10, 398 runs, never covered by the 135 labeled_dataset.json records)

batch_3_fresh.source: stage_lr/harvest_batch3.py -- 30 fresh, previously-unused sentences x 4 existing profile templates, run through reformulate() for the first time (no unused existing corpus of the right shape was found)
batch_3_fresh.judging_method: claude_api_standard_method (stage_lr/judge_pairs.py, DECISION_LOG.md 2026-08-30-O) -- first batch judged this way, not manually

pairs.original_sentence: Before the 1980s, it was unclear whether the warming effect of increased greenhouse gases were stronger than the cooling effect of airborne particulates in air pollution.
pairs.reason: Both candidates are grammatically broken (missing the 'more ___ than' comparative form, a real defect already confirmed by this record's own human rating). But A retains a plausible intensity/magnitude sense, while B substitutes an unrelated semantic domain (fertility, not strength) for a physical-intensity comparison — a much larger meaning break on top of the shared grammar issue.

pairs.original_sentence: Small talk is a bonding ritual and a strategy for managing interpersonal distance.
pairs.reason: Both are grammatical. 'Way' is generic and loses the 'deliberate technique/approach' sense of 'strategy'. 'Scheme' keeps that deliberate-plan sense more precisely, despite a mild negative-connotation risk ('scheming') the original doesn't carry.

pairs.original_sentence: An ontology is the set of objects, relations, concepts, and properties used by a particular domain of knowledge.
pairs.reason: A ('places') is a severe, nonsensical substitution — locations have nothing to do with an ontology's attributes. B ('constructs') stays correctly within the abstract/conceptual technical register the sentence needs.

pairs.original_sentence: A rational agent has goals or preferences and take actions to make them happen.
pairs.reason: Both drift from 'preferences', but 'options' shifts to an external-availability sense (what's on offer) while 'orientations' stays closer to an internal-disposition sense (what one favors) — a smaller category error for describing what an agent 'has' as a goal-driver.

pairs.original_sentence: Machine learning is the study of programs that can improve their performance on a given task automatically.
pairs.reason: A has a real countability/grammar error — 'software' is a mass noun in standard English, 'softwares' is non-standard pluralization (the same class of bug this project's own countability work targeted). B ('packages') is grammatical and a natural, common near-synonym for 'programs' in a computing context.

pairs.original_sentence: Between the 18th century and 1970 there was little net warming, as the warming impact of greenhouse gas emissions were offset by cooling from sulfur dioxide emissions.
pairs.reason: A produces an awkward duplicate ('gas gas emissions') but the surviving phrase 'gas emissions' stays coherent and climate-relevant. B ('building gas emissions') is not a real, coherent technical concept — a larger meaning break despite reading more smoothly on the surface.

pairs.original_sentence: The upper atmosphere is cooling, because greenhouse gases are trapping heat near the Earth's surface, and so less heat is radiating into space.
pairs.reason: Same pattern as the other 'greenhouse' case in this set: A's 'gas gases are trapping heat' is repetitive but keeps a coherent, climate-relevant claim; B's 'building gases' is not an established or coherent concept, a larger meaning break.

pairs.original_sentence: Small talk consists of three main parts: a greeting, conversation, and a closing.
pairs.reason: Both grammatical. 'Welcome' subtly shifts toward a hosting-specific connotation. 'Salutation' is the more precise, commonly interchangeable synonym for 'greeting' in this listing-of-parts context.

pairs.original_sentence: The phenomenon of small talk was initially studied in 1923 by Bronislaw Malinowski in his essay on the problem of meaning in primitive languages.
pairs.reason: 'Natural languages' collides with an unrelated, well-established linguistics term (human vs. constructed/formal language) — actively misleading in a sentence about linguistics. 'Naive' is an odd word choice for describing a language, but at least gestures toward the 'unsophisticated/simple' sense 'primitive' originally carried.

pairs.original_sentence: Machine learning is the study of programs that can improve their performance on a given task automatically.
pairs.reason: 'The work of programs' reads as 'produced/performed by programs' — a sense shift away from 'academic discipline'. 'The field of programs' keeps more of the discipline/domain sense 'study' carried, even if the phrasing is slightly awkward either way.

pairs.original_sentence: Fossil fuel use, deforestation, and some agricultural and industrial practices release greenhouse gases.
pairs.reason: Both are broken the same way — 'device'/'button' used as verbs make the sentence nonsensical. This is a real word-sense-disambiguation failure (the generator matched 'release' the noun/mechanism sense — as in a latch or trigger release — against a verb usage), not one candidate being better than the other. Useful as a negative example either way.

pairs.original_sentence: The Arctic has warmed the most, and temperatures on land have generally increased more than sea surface temperatures.
pairs.reason: 'Ocean' is a precise, close synonym for 'sea' in this earth-science context. 'Water' is a much broader, vaguer substitution that loses the specific marine meaning — a real instance of this project's own previously-diagnosed genericness bias (a more generic, higher-frequency word outranking a more precise one).

pairs.original_sentence: Cooking can prevent many forborne illnesses that would otherwise occur if raw food is consumed.
pairs.reason: A ('new food') is an unrelated, severe meaning substitution that destroys the food-safety-relevant distinction the sentence depends on (raw = uncooked, not 'new'). B ('uncooked') is essentially the exact intended meaning.

pairs.original_sentence: Cooking is done both by people in their own dwellings and by professional cooks and chefs in restaurants and other food establishments.
pairs.reason: Another genericness-bias case: 'buildings' is far too broad (loses the food-service meaning entirely, and reads oddly next to 'other food establishments'). 'Eateries' is accurate, natural, and fits the sentence.

pairs.original_sentence: In a business meeting, it enables people to establish each other's reputation and level of expertise.
pairs.reason: 'Esteem' is an imperfect but plausible, neutral-to-positive substitute. 'Notoriety' specifically implies negative fame — an incorrect connotation shift in a positive, professional-networking context.

pairs.original_sentence: Early researchers developed algorithms that imitated step-by-step reasoning that humans use when solving puzzles or making logical deductions.
pairs.reason: 'Detailed reasoning' is natural and stays in a related 'thoroughness' sense even without capturing sequentiality. 'Gradual reasoning' is an unusual, less coherent collocation that drifts toward an unrelated temporal-pace meaning.

pairs.original_sentence: Can you please review these three documents before Friday?
pairs.reason: 'Critique' is a very common, natural request verb for reviewing written documents. 'Inspect' carries a more formal/compliance-oriented connotation (inspecting a building, a product) that's a less natural register fit for this everyday request.

pairs.original_sentence: Digestion involves the breakdown of food into smaller and smaller components, until they can be absorbed and assimilated into the body.
pairs.reason: A creates an awkward, confusing duplicate word ('absorbed and absorbed'). B avoids the repetition and 'imbibed' is a plausible, if slightly formal, near-synonym for taking in nutrients.

pairs.original_sentence: Most of the digestion of food takes place in the small intestine.
pairs.reason: 'Small bowel' is standard anatomical terminology for 'small intestine' — accurate and natural. 'Small gut' is a less natural collocation; 'gut' alone is the common usage, not usually modified by 'small'.

pairs.original_sentence: Water and some minerals are reabsorbed back into the blood in the large intestine.
pairs.reason: A ('assumed') is a severe, nonsensical meaning substitution — has nothing to do with being physically taken back into the blood. B ('absorbed') loses the 're-' nuance but preserves the core physical-process meaning coherently.

pairs.original_sentence: All forms of life require carbon, energy, and water as well as various other molecules.
pairs.reason: 'Compounds' stays within the correct chemical/biological domain, a plausible near-synonym for molecules. 'Units' is too generic and loses the specific chemical meaning entirely.

pairs.original_sentence: Animals require complex nutrients such as carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins, obtaining them by consuming other organisms.
pairs.reason: 'Beings' stays within a plausible 'living things' semantic space appropriate for organisms being consumed. 'Systems' is a severe, nonsensical substitution — you don't consume a system.

pairs.original_sentence: Nutrient deficiency may be caused by a sudden decrease in nutrient intake or by an inability to absorb essential nutrients.
pairs.reason: 'Quick decrease' and 'fast decrease' are both natural, accurate, near-synonymous substitutions for 'sudden' here — no meaningful quality difference.

pairs.original_sentence: At any instant of time, the net force on a body is equal to the body's acceleration multiplied by its mass or, equivalently, the rate at which the body's momentum is changing with time.
pairs.reason: A breaks the core physics meaning: 'the value at which momentum is changing' isn't coherent (a value doesn't have a rate; this loses the entire 'speed of change' concept 'rate' was expressing). B ('pace') is a natural, meaning-preserving substitution in this exact 'rate/pace at which X changes' construction.

pairs.original_sentence: If two bodies exert forces on each other, these forces have the same magnitude but opposite directions.
pairs.reason: Both are odd, but 'the like magnitude' at least gestures toward 'similar/equal' (an archaic but interpretable phrasing), while 'the one magnitude' reads as a clearer determiner/grammar error with less recoverable meaning.

pairs.original_sentence: A volcano is a vent or fissure in the crust of a planetary-mass object that allows hot lava, volcanic ash, and gases to escape from a magma chamber below the surface.
pairs.reason: A ('below the open') is nonsensical — 'the open' as a bare noun doesn't fit here. B ('below the layer'), while vague about which layer, stays within plausible geological-structure vocabulary.

pairs.original_sentence: Solar energy can only be captured during the day, and ideally in cloudless conditions.
pairs.reason: A ('cloudless terms') uses the contract/agreement sense of 'terms', nonsensical for weather description. B ('cloudless states') stays closer to the intended condition/status meaning, even if slightly awkward.

pairs.original_sentence: In general, a program is an algorithm only if it stops eventually.
pairs.reason: 'Quits' is the natural, common way to describe a program/algorithm terminating. 'Discontinues' is accurate but carries a register mismatch, more typical of product lines than execution halting.

pairs.original_sentence: The probability of getting an outcome of head-head is 1 out of 4 outcomes, or, in numerical terms, 1/4, 0.25 or 25%.
pairs.reason: 'Quantitative' is a more precise semantic match for 'numerical' (expressed as numbers/quantities) than 'mathematical', which names a broader field. Both work, but B is the closer fit.

pairs.original_sentence: The first self-proclaimed civil engineer was John Smeaton, who constructed the Eddystone Lighthouse.
pairs.reason: Both substitute an unrelated sense of 'civil' for its 'civil engineering' technical/proper-noun-adjacent meaning — 'official' invents a status the original didn't have, 'polite' uses the courtesy sense entirely wrongly. A genuine word-sense-disambiguation failure either way.

pairs.original_sentence: She said she might be a little late because of traffic.
pairs.reason: 'Told' is transitive and needs an object ('told them') — 'told she might be late' is a harder grammar violation. 'Expressed' is mildly awkward (missing 'that') but a smaller violation.

pairs.original_sentence: He mentioned that he'd probably need more time to finish the report.
pairs.reason: 'Maybe' and 'likely' are both natural, accurate substitutes for 'probably' here — no clear quality difference.

pairs.original_sentence: The professor explained the concept twice before moving on to the next topic.
pairs.reason: 'Prof' preserves the specific role meaning (professor) despite being informal in register. 'Academic' is broader — loses the specific 'teacher explaining a concept' role implication.

pairs.original_sentence: The professor explained the concept twice before moving on to the next topic.
pairs.reason: 'Faculty' is typically a collective noun (a body of professors/a department), so 'the faculty explained' introduces a confusing single-vs-collective mismatch for describing one professor. 'Academic' is grammatically clean, even though it loses some role-specificity.

pairs.original_sentence: The exam covers everything we studied in the first six chapters.
pairs.reason: 'Examined' preserves the 'engaged with course material' sense of 'studied' more closely. 'Considered' drifts toward 'pondered', a mild sense weakening.

pairs.original_sentence: The manager asked everyone to submit their reports by the end of the day.
pairs.reason: A ('take their reports') is close to a meaning reversal — take and submit are near-opposite transfer directions. B ('propose their reports') is imprecise but at least preserves an offering/presenting directionality.

pairs.original_sentence: We're understaffed this week, so deadlines might slip a little.
pairs.reason: A ('deadlines might trip') is a category error — deadlines can't physically stumble, nonsensical. B ('deadlines might decline') carries a directional/negative-shift sense at least loosely compatible with 'slip'.

pairs.original_sentence: The team meets every Monday to review what went wrong the previous week.
pairs.reason: 'The past week' is completely natural and standard. 'The old week' is not idiomatic English — weeks aren't described as 'old' this way.

pairs.original_sentence: We didn't have enough time to see everything, so we skipped the museum.
pairs.reason: (Note: 'skipped'->'missed' also changed in both sentences, held constant across A and B, not part of this comparison.) 'View everything' fits the museum-exhibit context slightly more naturally than 'watch everything', which implies more sustained/continuous observation.

pairs.original_sentence: The soup tastes better the next day once the flavors have had time to develop.
pairs.reason: A ('time to produce') is grammatically incomplete — 'produce' is transitive and needs an object here. B ('time to grow') is natural, idiomatic, and grammatically sound for flavors developing.

pairs.original_sentence: The bakery down the street makes breads that's noticeably fresher than the supermarket's.
pairs.reason: 'Down the road' is completely natural and idiomatic. 'Down the neighborhood' is a non-standard, awkward collocation (you'd say 'in the neighborhood').

pairs.original_sentence: She apologized for showing up late to the party.
pairs.reason: A is essentially the same word (British spelling variant 'apologised'), perfectly natural. B ('excused for') has a real grammar error — 'excused' normally needs a reflexive object ('excused herself').

pairs.original_sentence: It's considered impolite to interrupts someone while they're speaking.
pairs.reason: 'Regarded' is a much closer semantic match to 'considered' (both mean viewed/thought of as). Both have a minor missing-preposition issue ('regarded/taken AS impolite'), but 'taken impolite' reads as more broken than 'regarded impolite'.

pairs.original_sentence: They've been friends since childhood, even though they don't see each other often now.
pairs.reason: 'Find each other' is an imperfect but plausible reading (locating time to meet). 'Play each other' introduces a wrong competitive/sports sense entirely inappropriate for old friends socializing.

pairs.original_sentence: Everyone was surprised when she declined the invitation.
pairs.reason: 'Shocked' preserves the surprise-emotion meaning closely (a stronger degree, same direction). 'Impressed' substitutes an unrelated, different emotional response (admiration, not being caught off guard).

pairs.original_sentence: It's normal to feels nervous before meeting someone for the first time.
pairs.reason: Both substitutions introduce the identical missing-article grammar error ('meeting person'/'meeting individual' instead of 'meeting A person'/'AN individual') — no quality difference between the two words themselves.

pairs.original_sentence: The old house had a narrow staircase that creaked with every step.
pairs.reason: (Note: 'creaked'->'noised' also changed in both sentences, held constant across A and B, not part of this comparison.) A ('a narrow stairs') has a real number-agreement error — 'stairs' is plural, mismatching the singular article. B ('a narrow stairway') is grammatically clean and a natural, accurate synonym.

pairs.original_sentence: The car's engine made a strange noise whenever it idled for too long.
pairs.reason: A ('a weird noise') is natural, accurate, near-perfect. B ('a other noise') has both a grammar error (a/an mismatch) and a meaning shift toward 'different/additional' rather than 'unusual'.

pairs.original_sentence: Turn off the power before you attempt to replace the light fixture.
pairs.reason: 'Substitute' is imperfectly phrased (usually needs 'for'/'with') but retains the core 'swap out' meaning of replace. 'Regenerate' substitutes a completely different concept — regrowth/restoration, not replacement with something new.

pairs.original_sentence: Press and hold the button for five seconds until the light turns green.
pairs.reason: (Note: 'seconds'->'times' also changed in both sentences, held constant across A and B, not part of this comparison.) Both substitute a verb-like/action word for what should be a physical object noun (the button itself), producing similarly awkward 'press and hold the [verb]' constructions. Neither is clearly better, though 'push' has some loose association with 'push-button'.

pairs.original_sentence: Assemble the shelf according to the numbered steps in the manual.
pairs.reason: Both substitute the literal/physical-walking sense of 'step' (paces, footsteps) for its procedural/sequential sense in a manual — a genuine word-sense failure either way, not one candidate being clearly better.

pairs.original_sentence: I think the new update make the ape harder to use, not easier.
pairs.reason: 'Believe' is a precise, natural synonym for 'think' as an opinion marker. 'Mean' serves a different discourse function (clarifying/rephrasing a prior statement), a real functional meaning shift.

pairs.original_sentence: Most of the town's residents work in the two factories nearby.
pairs.reason: A ('manufacturings') has a real grammar error — 'manufacturing' is normally uncountable, this pluralization is non-standard. B ('manufactories') is a real, grammatically valid (if old-fashioned) word meaning factories.

pairs.original_sentence: There are more public parks on the east side of the city than on the west.
pairs.reason: 'Municipality' is administratively accurate and doesn't imply a smaller scale (a city is a type of municipality). 'Town' introduces an unwarranted scale-down assumption relative to 'city'.

pairs.original_sentence: The store doesn't open until ten, but the café next door opens earlier.
pairs.reason: A ('opens newer') is nonsensical — 'newer' relates to recency of existence, not time-of-day, a wrong-sense substitution. B ('opens earliest') has a comparative/superlative mismatch but stays within the correct 'opening time' semantic domain.

pairs.original_sentence: Fleming went to Loudoun Moor School and Darvel School, and earned a two-year scholarship to Kilmarnock Academy before moving to London, where he attended the Royal Polytechnic Institution.
pairs.reason: A ('earned a two-year studies') has a real singular/plural agreement error. B ('earned a two-year aid') is a little ambiguous in its 'to' attachment but avoids that grammar problem and stays closer to the 'financial support' meaning of scholarship.

pairs.original_sentence: Fleming went to Loudoun Moor School and Darvel School, and earned a two-year scholarship to Kilmarnock Academy before moving to London, where he attended the Royal Polytechnic Institution.
pairs.reason: A ('earned a two-year learning') has an awkward countability issue (learning is normally uncountable) and shifts meaning toward 'knowledge gained' rather than 'financial award'. B ('aid') retains the financial-support sense central to 'scholarship'.

pairs.original_sentence: His elder brother, Tom, was already a physician and suggested that he should follow the same career.
pairs.reason: 'Indicated' is grammatically clean and a reasonably close synonym for 'suggested'. 'Informed that' has a mild missing-object awkwardness (usually 'informed HIM that'), a smaller but real quality gap.

pairs.original_sentence: Grandpa always tells the same story about his first fishing trip.
pairs.reason: "identical" preserves the meaning and reads naturally, while "aforementioned" wrongly implies the story was previously mentioned in this discourse and is oddly formal/legalistic in register.

pairs.original_sentence: The recipe requires precise measurements for the sauce to thicken properly.
pairs.reason: "accurate measurements" is grammatical and preserves the meaning; "very measurements" is ungrammatical since "very" cannot modify a noun this way.

pairs.original_sentence: He forgot his umbrella again despite the forecast predicting heavy rain.
pairs.reason: Both drop the needed "for" ("calling/guessing heavy rain"), but "calling for heavy rain" is a near-miss to a standard forecasting idiom, whereas "guessing" wrongly implies the forecast is uncertain speculation rather than a prediction.

pairs.original_sentence: The museum's new exhibit features artifacts from ancient trading routes.
pairs.reason: "trading paths" is a natural, meaning-preserving synonym for routes, while "trading lines" is awkward and risks being misread as financial/credit lines.

pairs.original_sentence: Prices for groceries have risen sharply over the past few months.
pairs.reason: "climbed sharply" is an idiomatic, natural collocation for price increases; "grown sharply" is grammatical but a less natural pairing with "sharply."

pairs.original_sentence: Her thesis argues that early exposure to music improves language development.
pairs.reason: "dissertation" is a close, natural synonym for "thesis" in academic register; "treatise" shifts the meaning toward a different genre of writing not necessarily original research.

pairs.original_sentence: The coach benched the striker after he missed three straight practices.
pairs.reason: "trainings" (though slightly nonstandard as a plural) still reads as practice sessions, while "exercises" changes the meaning to sound like individual drills or problems rather than sessions attended.

pairs.original_sentence: A sudden gust of wind knocked over the outdoor market stalls.
pairs.reason: "a sharp gust" is an idiomatic phrase that keeps the sense of abruptness; "a fast gust" shifts the meaning toward speed rather than suddenness and is less natural.

pairs.original_sentence: The startup raised significant funding to expand its engineering team.
pairs.reason: "meaningful funding" is grammatical though it drifts slightly from "substantial amount" toward "purposeful"; "meaning funding" is outright ungrammatical.

pairs.original_sentence: She switched careers after realizing accounting wasn't fulfilling.
pairs.reason: "flipped careers" is an odd but parseable metaphorical extension of switching; "operated careers" is nonsensical and distorts the meaning entirely.

excluded_multi_word_contaminated.note: These records DID produce a genuine second candidate for the targeted word, but because the source sentence has 2+ words flagged by the same profile, and substitution ranking is CONTEXTUAL (scored against the sentence as it's being progressively rebuilt), regenerating one word's candidate legitimately shifted which candidate ranked best for the OTHER flagged word too. That means candidate_A and candidate_B sentences differ in more than one place — not a clean, single-variable comparison, so these are excluded from the judged set above rather than forced into a format that misrepresents what actually varied. Not a script bug: confirmed by direct token-level diff, and the same underlying interaction this project's own R32 investigation named for the frozen pipeline's own candidate selection. (Batch 2, R10 source, added same guardrail: 32 more excluded here.)
